articles.title: Bring your buckets: DSWD to give away water filtration devices amid El Niño
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is preparing to distribute free water filtration devices as a part of the government"s response to the El Niño phenomenon, promising to teach…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 3:31pm

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is preparing to distribute free water filtration devices as a part of the government’s response to the El Niño phenomenon, promising to teach communities how to use them.

This follows President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s viral “balde” or bucket remark, which the Palace later explained was a part of rain collection and water purification. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro even promised that DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian himself would demonstrate how to properly use them.

A day later, Gatchalian was at Malacañang Palace where he demonstrated how to use the DSWD’s water filtration kit. There he announced that the agency will roll out these kits because of the expected harsher El Niño that will last until 2027.

“Next week, imbitahan namin kayo. We have the first session kung saan aanyayahan namin iyong mga communities. Dalhin nila iyong balde nila, bubutasan namin, lalagyan ng filter, tuturuan rin. May session doon kung paano linisin. Mabilis lang na proseso then later on, iyong kit na mismo ang ibibigay natin,” Gatchalian said in a press conference on Wednesday.

(Next week, we invite you. We have the first session where we will invite the communities. Bring their buckets, we will drill a hole in them, install the filter. We have a session on how to clean it. It is a fast process and later on, we will give them the kit.)
There is also a larger version of the water filtration device, which is typically used for communities. It is a rain catcher that filters the water in larger portions.

The agency will start distributing the water filtration kits and installing the large versions in various communities, but Gatchalian said that they will prioritize areas that have already declared a state of calamity because of the El Niño phenomenon.
Gatchalian said that the kits are free, funded by the agency’s quick response funds.
Asked why the government was only distributing these kits now and not during the rainy season when there was more rain, Gatchalian said that these devices were mainly used during emergencies.
“Sayang naman ang government resources kapag binigay namin iyong mga filter na walang pangangailangan,” Gatchalian said.
(It would be a waste of government resources if we gave these filters away when there was no need.)

The DSWD Chief guaranteed that the water was clean, as it was also certified by the Department of Health as a medical device. Gatchalian, together with other officials from the DSWD, provided a live demonstration of the device.

They brought out a standard, plastic bucket and drilled a hole in it to install the water filtration system. The officials then brought out water mixed with dirt and poured it into the bucket with the filtration device.
The water that came out appeared to be clear during the demonstration.
Gatchalian and Castro also drank the water to show that it was safe, and even distributed samples to reporters present.

The water filtration system they have is from the non-government organization Waves for Water, according to Gatchalian. It is typically part of the emergency kits they give away during emergencies. During emergencies, the DSWD also gives away buckets where people can install the water filtration system.
Gatchalian stressed that these are only parts of the government’s ongoing efforts to address the El Niño phenomenon.
The prevailing El Niño phenomenon is expected to be record-breaking, with state meteorologists warning of negative impacts to agriculture and other industries. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: [In This Economy] Will Sara Duterte be good for business and the economy?
articles.summary: Until now, Sara Duterte has said little about her specific plans or vision for the country, as well as economic reforms and policies she might put in place in case she wins

items: Vice President Sara Duterte faces impeachment trial allegations of undeclared wealth, business interests, and connections to drug trafficking, raising questions about her credibility and future political aspirations.

Despite her calls for human rights, accountability, and a predictable business environment, her family's controversial history and her own impeachment raise doubts about her commitment to these principles.

Critics argue that her recent speech reflects hypocrisy, as she distances herself from the failures of her father's administration while failing to provide a clear vision for her potential presidency in 2028.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Juicy revelations recently surfaced in the Senate impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, including alleged undeclared wealth that could reach P1.5 billion, continuing business interests (banned by the Constitution), and even supposed remittances from China and Hong Kong to a company linked to Duterte’s husband.

The evidence is so overwhelming that the chances of a conviction seem to have spiked, at least from where I sit. In fact, as of Tuesday, October 13, the prosecution dropped 3 of 4 impeachment charges, seemingly confident that the remaining one on unexplained wealth can stand on its own.
Until there is conviction, though, Sara Duterte continues to be a contender in the 2028 elections. In fact, based on the latest polling data, she’s a frontrunner.

The problem that bugs me is that until now, Sara Duterte has said little about her specific plans or vision for the country, as well as economic reforms and policies she might put in place in case she wins.

On October 13, she had an opportunity to lay out those plans at the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s 52nd Philippine Business Conference and Expo (watch video below), held at the Manila Hotel. There, she called for respect for human rights, accountable government, and businesses free from political harassment. She also demanded integrity and competence from public officials.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Will Sara Duterte be good for business and the economy?

blocks.text: But are these exhortations credible? How did the Dutertes (Rodrigo and Sara) measure up to these standards when they had the power to put them into practice?
Let’s start with a pretty bold statement: VP Sara said, “Imagine a Philippines where human rights are upheld, justice is fair, laws are applied and respected.”

This one is jarring to hear because of everything that happened in her father’s drug war (2016–2022). Thousands were killed, possibly more than 30,000, and various human rights organizations documented widespread killings, arbitrary detention, and persistent impunity. All this culminated in the historic arrest in March 2025 of Rodrigo Duterte, who now awaits trial at The Hague.

Will Sara do a repeat of the drug war? Will Sara assure the victims of the drug war that there will be no repeat, and that those who perpetrated abuses during her father’s regime will be held to account? Her speech offered no assurance that those abuses would never happen again.

A few days ago, Thai authorities intercepted a drug shipment that’s supposed to be headed to the Philippines. VP Sara said in response: “We recognize the concerns surrounding the Philippines’ role in regional drug trafficking and express my deep regret that our country has become associated with this problem.”

But during the impeachment trial, a bank witness testified that funds from Sara and Rodrigo Duterte’s joint account were used to purchase a manager’s check payable to Samuel “Sammy” Uy, whom former senator Antonio Trillanes IV has accused of involvement in the drug trade.

In the PCCI speech, Sara also spoke of the need for people to freely express their opinions. Yet her father repeatedly threatened ABS-CBN over its franchise. In 2020, the broadcaster was ordered off the air after its franchise expired, and a House committee rejected its renewal. The Palace claimed neutrality despite Duterte’s very public hostility. Apart from this, Duterte also attacked Rappler and filed trumped-up charges left and right.

Sara also asked her audience to imagine businesses that need not give to politicians just to be safe from harassment. She added: “Policies should be predictable. Businesses and individuals can plan for the future without fearing arbitrary government decisions.”
But exactly the opposite happened during her father’s time. Policies were weaponized against Duterte’s perceived enemies, and Duterte infamously cursed and railed against prominent businesspeople.

Who would forget Duterte’s capricious and abrupt closure of Boracay Island to tourists in 2018? Then in December 2019, Rodrigo Duterte threatened to jail the people behind Manila Water and Maynilad over their concession agreements. He also floated a military takeover of their operations. Sure, water contracts deserve scrutiny, but the government could’ve reviewed them through lawful processes without threatening businesspeople with imprisonment.

This is what one might call “economic lawlessness,” and it’s a major turnoff for potential investors. Think about it: why commit money to a project that takes years to pay off if the president can threaten your company and upend its dealings with government? Such uncertainty makes investments riskier and political connections more valuable.
Does Sara now think her father’s threats were wrong? Would she keep personal grudges out of regulatory decisions? These are basic questions for someone promising a predictable business environment.
Sara also declared that leaders should be open to investigation and held responsible for misconduct. Corruption, she said, drains resources from essential services.
But this is precisely the reason why she’s been impeached not once but twice. Her father’s track record in this regard is also questionable.

Recall the Senate investigation into pandemic procurement involving Pharmally. In October 2021, Rodrigo Duterte directed executive officials and employees to stop attending the Senate blue ribbon committee’s hearings on the 2020 Commission on Audit report. His government denied corruption allegations while obstructing the basic scrutiny that should have tested them.

Meanwhile, Sara also has her own spending to explain, and this brings us to the current impeachment trial at the Senate. Her office spent P125 million in confidential funds in 11 days in 2022. State auditors disallowed roughly P73 million for violating confidential-fund rules, findings her camp contests. Sure, spending quickly alone proves no wrongdoing, and an audit disallowance is no criminal conviction. But how does she reconcile these findings with her talk of integrity?

On education, Sara called for capable teachers and quality learning. As education secretary from 2022 to 2024, however, she defended a P150-million confidential-fund request for 2024 on national-security grounds, before eventually dropping it. Why prioritize secret spending in an agency struggling to provide the basics of education?

Her father’s education record was disastrous as well. By August 2021, UNICEF reported that the Philippines was among only five countries that had not started in-person classes since the pandemic began. More than 27 million students were affected by the prolonged school closures, which meant lost learning and poorer prospects for future earnings and our economy’s productivity.
Sara’s concerns about the cost of living, jobs, and public services also invite a closer look at the previous Duterte administration.

In my new book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and Covid-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, I examine how her father’s governance compounded the pandemic’s damage. COVID-19 hit countries around the world. How to protect livelihoods and keep essential services working depended on government decisions, and to this day Duterte hasn’t answered for this.

Even before COVID-19, Filipino households suffered under Rodrigo Duterte through the 2018 inflation surge. Higher world oil prices and food-supply problems contributed, while the administration’s excise-tax increases added to prices.

Sure, the current Marcos administration deserves criticism for its failures. But is VP Sara well placed to do this? What exactly in her track record suggests that she can do a much better job, if at all? She needs to explain her own decisions and tell us which of her father’s policies she would continue or abandon.

All in all, VP Sara’s speech on October 13 amounts to breathtaking hypocrisy. At the same time she turns on the current Marcos administration, she turns a blind eye to the disastrous presidency of her own father—and also the many red flags in her own track record.
This country already paid dearly for twin plagues from 2016 to 2022, namely Duterte and COVID-19. We can’t afford a third plague come 2028 in the form of yet another Duterte. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 3:29pm
Senator Loren Legarda has filed for an extended medical leave for October 12 and 13, 2026, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug said Wednesday.
According to Bantug, Legarda has no advice yet regarding her attendance in the Senate for the remaining days of October and for November.
Legarda has been on extended medical leave since August 3. The last time she was seen at the Senate was on July 29, during the plenary session.
Session at the Senate is currently adjourned and will resume on November 9.

Legarda’s spokesperson, Atty. Tony La Viña, previously said the senator was undergoing medical treatment in France for a lung and autoimmune condition and was taking time to rest, as her condition worsens under stress or tension.

Legarda and her son, Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste, are facing complaints for plunder and graft in connection with the alleged failure of the latter’s renewable energy firm to provide solar power, as mandated in its congressional franchise.
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin "Boying" Remulla said that the senator is included in the case because Leviste was able to secure the franchise while she was the Senate Finance chair in 2019.
Legarda has denied the allegations, saying she has always upheld her integrity. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Russian strikes leave 600,000 without power in Ukraine, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Ukraine's president says "critical" infrastructure was hit overnight, while emergency services say at least three were killed.

blocks.text: At least 600,000 people across Ukraine are now without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region and also in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv - despite a claim by US President Donald Trump on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
In Kyiv, at least three people were killed and 21 injured, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.
Russia's defence ministry said its "massive" strikes overnight had targeted communications and energy facilities in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions used by Ukraine's military.

The defence ministry also said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea - Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine's air force said that overnight, Russia had launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones, and that four of those missiles and 115 drones had been shot down.
On Sunday, Trump wrote in a post on social media: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
President Zelensky has since repeatedly said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.

But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Video recording device found in cabin of HMAS Leeuwin navy ship in Cairns
articles.summary:
Defence announcement comes after Jacqui Lambie tells parliament a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on board

A “video recording device” was found in the cabin of an…

blocks.text: A “video recording device” was found in the cabin of a Royal Australian Navy ship in Cairns, the defence department has revealed, just hours after senator Jacqui Lambie alleged in parliament that a camera had been found concealed in a women’s shower on the vessel.

The department confirmed on Wednesday afternoon that a device had been found aboard the HMAS Leeuwin three days earlier. In a statement after Guardian Australia had contacted the department for response to Lambie’s allegations, a spokesperson said police were investigating, but did not reveal further details about where the device was located.
“On 11 October 2026, Defence became aware that a video recording device had been located in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin, while alongside in Cairns, Queensland,” they said.

“The incident was referred to the Joint Military Police Unit and Defence is working with civilian authorities. Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form.”

On Wednesday morning, Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate that she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.
“The sender told me that concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors’ showers facilities on the vessel HMAS Leeuwin, based in Cairns,” she said in the Senate.

“I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered.

“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask Navy.”

Guardian Australia asked the department if any perpetrator had been identified, if the defence force was aware of hidden cameras being found in other navy facilities, and if any such footage from hidden cameras had been found to have been shared online.

The department did not directly answer those questions. In its statement, it said HMAS Leeuwin had “remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship’s crew”.
after newsletter promotion

“The welfare of individuals remains Defence’s priority, and support is ongoing. As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time,” it said.
Asked at a subsequent press conference about the incident, Lambie said she was unhappy with the department’s response.

“Defence needs to know this. Your people had a gutful, and if there was abuse going on, they’re now coming to me. OK, I’m right on their tail. Enough is enough. Get control of what is going on in the defence force,” she said.

“What I want to know is, have they gone around on the rest of those boats, the subs, whatever, and had a look and make sure there’s no other cameras? Because we are not sure whether it’s coming from contractors that go on them, or whether it’s come from defence members.”

Senator Loren Legarda left the country with her son, Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste, on August 2
MANILA, Philippines — Senator Loren Legarda has again extended her medical leave, this time until October 13, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. confirmed.

This is the latest medical leave filed by Legarda, who first left the country with her son, Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste, on August 2. This was days after plunder and graft complaints were announced against them by the Office of the Ombudsman over the latter’s solar energy projects.
Legarda first filed for medical leave from August 3 to 5, and has been extending it since then.

The senator previously confirmed that she had filed for medical leave with the Senate and asked the public “not to draw unwarranted conclusions from my travel or link it to the recent false and baseless allegations, which undeservedly besmirch a reputation that I have built over decades of public service.”

Legarda and three other senators — Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta who are detained over plunder charges, and Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa who is in hiding over an International Criminal Court warrant of arrest — have stopped receiving salaries as they remain absent from plenary sessions of the Senate and the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte's camp questions Senate majority's 'lack of outrage' over dropped articles
articles.summary: Sara Duterte"s camp questions Senate majority"s 'lack of outrage" over dropped articles

blocks.text: The spokesperson for Vice President Sara Duterte on Wednesday questioned the supposed silence and “lack of outrage” by the senator-judges in the majority over the decision of the House prosecution panel to withdraw three of the four impeachment articles.

Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. claimed that approximately P500 million---or P25 million per day---was used by the Senate over a span of 20 trial days for Articles I and IV. Considering other expenses, and the “wasted salaries” of members of the Congress who participated in the trial, he said the public cost for hearing the dropped articles would exceed P1 billion.

“What is equally troubling, however, is the lack of outrage by the Senate majority. Hindi ba nasayang ang oras ninyo? Hindi ba kayo nanghihinayang na nagamit sana ang panahon para tugunan ang mga kritikal na pangangailangan ng bansa? Hindi ba kayo nagagalit na nagwaldas ang prosekusyon ng perang kasing laki o mas malaki pa sa confidential funds na linustay diumano ni VP Sara, na hanggang ngayon at kailanman ay hindi nila mapapatunayan?” Panelo asked.

(Wasn’t your time wasted? Don’t you regret that the time could have been used to address the critical needs of the country? Aren’t you outraged that the prosecution wasted money as big or bigger than the confidential funds allegedly embezzled by VP Sara, which they have never been able to prove to this day?)
“Who is going to hold them accountable? A judge in a regular court would have at least given the prosecution a proper tongue lashing for wasting its time if this happened there,” he added.
Duterte’s spokesman further asked if the silence of some of the senator-judges had anything to do with the upcoming 2028 national elections.

“So why the quiet? Is it because the goal to disqualify the leading presidential candidate in 2028 justifies the means? Is it because the numbers for conviction are already locked in under the lower threshold? Is it because a longer trial risks shifting those numbers, making a faster resolution preferable? Is it because convicting the Vice President earlier may reduce the damage to Senator-Judges seeking elective posts in 2028?”
“The silence is deafening. Huwag naman kayong masyadong halata (don't be too obvious),” he continued.
'What does he want me to do?'
Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, chairman of the Senate Committee on Accounts, in return, asked Panelo where he got his figures that the upper chamber supposedly spent P25 million per day.

“As far as I know, the [General Appropriations Act] 2025 budget for the impeachment trial, most of which has remained unspent, only roughly P2 million was disbursed for the judges’ robes and other items, is now being used under the ‘continuing appropriations’ provision in the GAA,” Lacson said.

“I wasn’t referring to the trial, but the legislative functions of the Senate and my basis was the Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses and Personnel Service for one year which I extrapolated on a per day basis,” he added.
Senator Joel Villanueva, meanwhile, expressed that he simply wanted to make sure that his interjections during the trial are fair.

“What does he want me to do? Magwala ako? Na i-feel ko na ako 'yung pinaparinggan? (does he want me to go on a rampage and say that I feel alluded to?) I don't think so. We are a court… I can look at all of you eye to eye, sa mga questions that I raised, wala akong…everything that I have done so far, I'm very careful about it,” Villanueva said in an ambush interview.

“I wanted to make sure that it's fair. And I know that the entire country will be looking and listening and watching us. And I would still encourage them to watch us and scrutinize whatever we are doing here, because that's, of course, the beauty of democracy,” he added.
Senator Bong Go said that he could not speak on behalf of other senator-judges regarding the allegation of Duterte’s camp.
Regardless, he believes the presentation of evidence in the trial should be fair both for the prosecution and defense.

“Karapatan po ng prosecution ‘yan. Karapatan po ng korte to decide. Pero as one of the senator-judges, gusto natin makakita ng pantay o patas na laban. So, ibig sabihin, kung nakasuntok na ‘yung kabila, bigyan mo naman ng pagkakataon na lumaban naman ‘yung kabila nang patas,” Go said in an ambush interview.

(That is the right of the prosecution. It is also the court’s right to decide on that. But as one of the senator-judges, I want to see a fair fight. So, that means if one side has already landed a punch, the other side should also be given a fair chance to fight back.)
GMA News Online also reached out to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian for comment and will update this story once he responds. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech
articles.summary: Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smart watches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of…

image.caption: Cheap mini fans used for a month in summer are often end up forgotten at the bottom of a drawer or in the trash Image: Luis Soto/SOPA Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling.

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes.
"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

blocks.caption: Cheap e-vapes are part of the rising trend of fast tech that is adding to the growing e-waste crisis Image: Joel Carrett/AAP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.
This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.
The Great Wall of e-waste and what to do about it

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.
In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment.
Recycling rare earths in Germany to reduce China dependence
In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.
These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.
"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she told DW.
Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.
But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive.

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.
Healthcare's increasing digital waste problem
Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors, and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

blocks.caption: Even small, cheap electronics should be recycled as they contain valuable materials Image: Desmond Tiro/DW

blocks.text: A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.
That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.
"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.
How wearables are revolutionizing heart health

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."
A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

blocks.caption: Many digital health devices could be reused or recycled if designed properly Image: Marko Prpic/PIXSELL/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Green nudges' help citizens to recycle

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges"such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person, motivate people to "do the right thing."

articles.title: Suspected mastermind in Laos shabu shipment to Philippines identified — PDEA
articles.summary: Authorities have identified the suspected mastermind behind a major drug smuggling attempt intercepted in Laos over a week ago, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency said.

blocks.text: October 14, 2026 | 2:45pm

Motorists drive on a street under Lao national flags and Lao People's Revolutionary Party flags in Vientiane on December 2, 2025, during Lao National Day celebrations to mark 50 years of communist rule.

MANILA, Philippines — Authorities have identified the suspected mastermind behind a major drug smuggling attempt intercepted in Laos over a week ago, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) said Wednesday, October 14.

PDEA spokesperson Joseph Frederick Calulut said they already knew the names of all individuals involved in the case but refused to release any details about the alleged principal’s identity and background to avoid compromising the ongoing investigation.
“So alam na ho atin ‘yung mga pangalan nila at saka ‘yung mga account na ginamit ho nila,” Calulut said in an interview with Super Radyo dzBB.
(So, we already know their names and the accounts they used.)

Earlier, PDEA identified two Filipino individuals with the aliases “Fajad” and “Boyet” as the subjects of its investigation after Lao authorities busted an attempt to ship 521 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine, or shabu, to the Philippines via a private jet.
Fajad was arrested and detained in Laos, while Boyet had reportedly left the country.
‘Sam Gor’

Calulut said both Boyet and Fajad are allegedly linked to the major drug syndicate Sam Gor, which primarily operates in the Golden Triangle region, an infamous area for illicit drug production that covers the borders of three Southeast Asian nations: Myanmar, Laos and Thailand.
The confiscated drugs allegedly came from the Sam Gor syndicate, according to Calulut, who added that the group is responsible for distributing illegal drugs across the Asia-Pacific region.
Boyet and Fajad are allegedly Sam Gor’s links based in Mindanao.

Calulut said Sam Gor uses maritime routes through the Andaman Sea and the Strait of Malacca for drug distribution and targets Mindanao as an entry point to the Philippines, making the region’s residents more vulnerable to the syndicate.
The PDEA spokesperson said the agency remains in coordination with other concerned units and foreign counterparts to track Boyet and crack down on illegal drug trade operations in Mindanao.
“Ito naman ho ay kino-coordinate naman natin sa ating mga foreign counterparts para ma-track pa rin ho natin kahit nasa ibang bansa na po siya,” Calulut said.
(We are coordinating with our foreign counterparts so we can continue tracking him even if he is already in another country.)

Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building and 17 arrest warrants had been issued in the raid linked to the channel's owner.

Meanwhile, Istanbul's popular Mayor Ekrem Imamoğlu, widely seen as Erdoğan's biggest political rival, has been in prison for over a year over corruption accusations. He denies all the charges.

articles.title: Malacañang on dropping articles in Sara Duterte impeachment trial: That's prosecution's strategy
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday said it will not question the legal strategy of the House prosecution panel to withdraw three of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 2:18pm
Malacañang on Wednesday said it will not question the legal strategy of the House prosecution panel to withdraw three of the four Articles of Impeachment leveled against Vice President Sara Duterte.

“Well everybody, we are all for the truth, we are all for transparency and accountability. Pero kung ito ang legal na estratehiya ng prosecution, hindi po natin maku-kwestyon kung anuman ang kanilang desisyon,” Palace Press Officer Usec. Claire Castro said.
(Well we are all for the truth, we are all for transparency and accountability. But if this is the prosecution’s legal strategy, we cannot question whatever decision they have made.)
“Kung ‘yun po ang nakikita nila, sila naman ang mga prosecutors, so mas kabisado po nila kung ano ‘yung mas malakas nila na mga ebidensya,” she added.
(If that is how the prosecution sees it, then so be it. After all, they are the prosecutors, so they are the ones who know which pieces of evidence are stronger.)

During the trial on Tuesday, the prosecution manifested that they would no longer pursue Articles I, III and IV against the Vice President, detailing allegations of misuse of confidential funds, bribery, and grave threats.

With the decision, the prosecution would only push for Article II, which concerns allegations that Duterte failed to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.
The Senate impeachment court has accepted the move by the prosecution to withdraw three of the four impeachment articles.
Castro said that the Vice President could address the allegations against her in other ways.
“Kung ano ang naipikta nilang (prosecution) mga ebidensya at mga dokumento, ‘yun siguro ang mananatili sa isipan natin,” she said.
(Whatever evidence and documents the prosecution has presented, that is likely what will remain in our minds.)

“Ang respondent na si Bise Presidente, ay maaari namang tugunan ito sa maraming pamamaraan. Sabi nga natin, kung noon pa…naipaliwanag ng Bise Presidente, especially patungkol sa confi funds, hindi na nga po siguro aabot sa impeachment trial,” she added.

(The respondent, the Vice President, could address these in various ways. As we’ve said, if the Vice President had addressed it earlier, especially the allegations regarding the confidential funds, it probably won’t even have to reach an impeachment trial.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Cardinal Tagle to lead Vatican Mass as Pope Leo recovers
articles.summary: Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle is set to preside over a Mass in Vatican City amid Pope Leo’s hospitalization following his medical procedure.

blocks.text: October 14, 2026 | 2:18pm

This photo taken and handout on May 18, 2025 by The Vatican Media shows Filipino cardinal Luis Antonio Gokim Tagle putting the Fisherman's Ring on a finger of Pope Leo XIV during a Holy mass for the beginning of his pontificate, in St Peter's square in The Vatican. (
MANILA, Philippines — Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle is set to preside over a Mass in Vatican City amid Pope Leo’s hospitalization following his medical procedure.
In a press conference on October 13 (Vatican time), Jesuit priest Giacomo Costa announced that Tagle is set to preside over the Mass at 10 a.m. (Vatican time).
According to the Vatican’s calendar, the Eucharistic celebration will conclude the meeting marking the 10th anniversary of the publication of the apostolic exhortation “Amoris Laetitia.”
The Mass will also include prayers for the Pope’s health and for families, according to Costa.
“He is going to preside over the Mass during which we will pray in a special way for the health of the Holy Father, as well as for all families and couples,” Costa said in Italian.
Tagle, the pro-prefect of the Dicastery for Evangelization, was also recently appointed dean of the College of Cardinals.
Tagle was the first Filipino and Asian to hold the said position, which is traditionally held by Europeans. He replaces Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re.

Meanwhile, the Vatican also announced that Pope Leo’s surgery to remove a lung nodule was successful. Doctors at Gemelli Hospital in Rome said, “The Pope woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor.”
However, the doctors also diagnosed the pontiff with lung adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer.

articles.title: Prosecution: Unexplained wealth charge alone in Sara Duterte impeach case worth the risk
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel said on Wednesday that pinning the impeachment case on just one article out of the entire Articles of Impeachment -- on Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged unexplained…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 2:14pm

The House prosecution panel said on Wednesday that pinning the impeachment case on just one article out of the entire Articles of Impeachment — on Vice President Sara Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth — is a risk worth taking.

House prosecutors Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Luistro and Bicol Saro Party-list Representative Terry Ridon made the position a day after the Senate impeachment court accepted the prosecution’s motion to withdraw three out of four Articles of Impeachment against the Vice President.

This was after prosecution witness and financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera testified that the Vice President and her husband Atty. Mans Carpio have an unexplained wealth ranging from P817 million to P1.5 billion based on forensic investigation of Duterte's Statement of Assets, of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) and their bank records, income tax documents and business interests records.

“If we don't get a conviction on this last article or remaining article, then that will be the end of this entire impeachment process. We are wiling to take that risk because we considered the impatience of the public, the challenging task of the impeachment court and ultimately, that will be beneficial as well on the part of the respondent Vice President,” Luistro, the House lead prosecutor, said in an interview on Super Radyo dzBB.

“We considered the previous impeachment cases against [former President Joseph] Estrada and [former Chief Justice Renato] Corona, so that option [of withdrawing certain Articles] has long been open to us. And when we saw [the evidence] on unexplained wealth, tumindi na ang pag-uusap [na] napakalakas nitong Article na ito, until we are able to come up with this decision,” Luistro added.
(And when we saw [the evidence] on unexplained wealth, the discussions centered on how strong this Article was, until we are able to come up with this decision,” she said.

Ridon then said that Cabrera’s testimony, alongside that of the officials from banks, insurance firm, Bureau of Internal Revenue and Anti-Money Laundering Council, of millions and billions worth of financial transactions involving the Vice President and her husband are too compelling not be be focused on.

“The unexplained wealth as testified by Atty. Cabrera is P817 million in a conservative estimate and P1.5 billion at his most liberal calculation. When the prosecutors discussed these numbers, we decided dito na tayo tumutok (let us focus on this). Ito po ang ebidensiya na kailangan (This is the evidence we need). We will rise or fall on the basis of unexplained wealth,” Ridon, one of the prosecutors for Article 2, said in a separate press conference.

“And let us not forget, their financial activities include P200,000 credit card bill for one dinner. Hindi ho lubos maisip ‘yan na puedeng mangyari sa isang ordinaryong Pilipino. Tatlong barangay na po ang puwedeng pakainin roon. That is why we have the righteous outrage over this evidence presented by Atty. Cabrera. That is, we have every justification to proceed with one Article and to have absolute faith on unexplained wealth as a singular Article [of impeachment] for this trial,” Ridon added.
(It is unthinkable that that could happen to an ordinary Filipino. That could have already fed three barangays.)

The House prosecution panel on Tuesday said there is no denial of due process for Duterte amid the prosecution’s sudden withdrawal of three out of four Articles of Impeachment against the Vice President because the defense was given a comprehensive time to question the prosecution witnesses.
Duterte however on Wednesday said the prosecution's withdrawal of three articles of impeachment on Tuesday is an admission that the allegations hurled against her lacked basis from the start.
"The withdrawal is an admission that the allegations lacked basis from the very beginning," Atty. Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., spokesperson for Duterte, said in a statement.

The three Articles of Impeachment withdrawn by the prosecution include: Article 1 on the misuse of P612 million of confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education (DepEd), Article 3 on bribery of DepEd officials during the Vice President’s tenure as Education Secretary, and Article 4 of grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. and his family members.
The prosecutors were able to present evidence on Article 4, 1 and 2 before they decided to withdraw Articles 1, 4 and 3.
Ahead of the withdrawal of the three Articles, the prosecution submitted a manifestation before the Impeachment court last October 6 that it will withdraw the Article 3 charge.

With the Impeachment court accepting the prosecution’s motion to drop the three impeachment Articles, the Impeachment court also ruled that the defense will no longer need to present evidence to response to these three allegations since there are no more charges to respond to.
The defense is expected to present its evidence on November 9. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Philippines backs global pledge against maritime tolls
articles.summary: The pledge, which was initiated by the European Union, was signed by all 27 member states and 33 other countries as they reaffirmed their support for freedom of navigation.

blocks.text: October 14, 2026 | 2:05pm

A China Coast Guard ship (R) sailing past a Philippine fishing boat with volunteers from the civilian-led mission Atin Ito (This Is Ours) Coalition on board, in the disputed South China Sea on May 16, 2024.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines has joined 59 other countries in opposing the introduction of new maritime tolls in vital waterways by signing a global pledge against any measure that could compromise lawful international navigation.
The pledge, initiated by the European Union (EU), was signed by all 27 member states and 33 other countries as they reaffirmed their support for freedom of navigation.
It came following previous reports indicating that authorities in Iran had imposed a maritime toll fee system in the Strait of Hormuz, causing disruptions in the waterway’s operations.

The pledge stressed that no government is allowed to impose maritime tolls under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), reiterating that such “discriminatory measures” would set a “dangerous precedent” for international waterways.

“No State should impose discriminatory limits on the passage of ships through such waterways in a manner inconsistent with international law, as reflected in UNCLOS. This principle is vital for global security,” the pledge read.

Through the pledge, the signatories committed to supporting “defensive and non-escalatory” multilateral actions to preserve freedom of navigation, rejecting “coercive or unilateral actions” that would undermine the international law of the sea, and opposing any measures that would disrupt lawful navigation in international shipping routes.
EU High Representative and Vice President Kaja Kallas announced the pledge on October 12, saying it was a ‘clear diplomatic signal’ to those attempting to ‘hijack’ international shipping routes.
“International waters, the arteries of our economy, must remain open to everyone, not to whoever can pay,” Kallas said in a press briefing in Luxembourg on October 12.

articles.title: Ukrainian soldier to go on trial over sabotage of Nord Stream gas pipelines
articles.summary:
Special forces officer Serhii Kuznetsov denies involvement in the 2022 blasts that left pipelines badly damaged

A Ukrainian soldier is to go on trial in Hamburg accused of taking part in…

blocks.text: A Ukrainian soldier is to go on trial in Hamburg accused of taking part in one of the most brazen acts of sabotage in postwar European history – the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany.

Serhii Kuznetsov, a special forces officer from the Ukrainian military, is accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services.

Kuznetsov, who will be identified in the trial opening on Wednesday just as Serhii K due to German privacy laws, was referenced by his full name in an extradition order. He is alleged to have prepared and carried out the detonation of at least four incendiary devices of up to 27kg in weight at a depth of about 80 metres under the Baltic Sea, close to the Danish island of Bornholm.

He is believed to have had six accomplices, including four deep-sea divers, an explosives expert and a ship’s captain, who are alleged to have used a rented yacht and timer-controlled explosives. Both he and his country deny any involvement in the attacks.

The explosions took place on 26 September 2022, badly damaging the pipelines which had been constructed to carry Russian natural gas between Vyborg in western Russia and Lubmin, near Greifswald in northern Germany.

blocks.caption: Gas bubbles from the Nord Stream 2 leak reach the surface of the Baltic sea near Bornholm in October 2022. Photograph: Danish Defence Command/Reuters

blocks.text: The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst. They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The attacks happened as European countries were seeking to transition away from Russian energy supplies in reaction to the Kremlin’s aggression.
They exposed the dependence of Europe – and, in particular, Germany – on Russian gas as well as highlighting the murkiness of underground operations during wartime.
Security observers initially blamed Moscow for the attack. Russia has denied involvement, in turn blaming the US, which has denied it just as forcefully.

However, in July German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.”
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved.

Kuznetsov was arrested in August 2025 on a family holiday in Italy, with Italian police reporting that he surrendered without resistance. He had been travelling on a false passport. He was extradited to Germany last November, after legal efforts to prevent this failed.

A further suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, an air conditioner installer and hobby diver, was arrested on a European warrant in northern Croatia in August. He is fighting his extradition to Germany having applied for asylum in Croatia. He denies any role in the sabotage.

Aware of how potentially incendiary the trial could be, with Ukraine effectively in the dock for a crime committed against its ally – and one of its staunchest wartime supporters – the German government has declined to comment on the trial.

The far-right populist, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland party, which is soaring in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream plot to boost its argument that German aid for Ukraine must cease and the pipeline be reinstated so that cheap supplies of gas can help counter the cost of living crisis.

The trial is attracting much attention, not least because Nord Stream was already a highly controversial issue before the attack, involving Russia’s leader, Vladimir Putin, who, with the then German chancellor, Gerhard Schröder, managed to bypass Ukraine as a transit country with Nord Stream 1. After Schröder left the chancellery, Putin appointed him as chair of the supervisory board of the company Nord Stream AG. Schröder was seen last week attending Putin’s birthday celebration.

blocks.caption: Former German chancellor Gerhard Schröder, pictured at Vladimir Putin’s birthday party last week, was appointed chair of Nord Stream AG’s supervisory board by Putin after he left the chancellery. Photograph: Kremlin.ru/Reuters

blocks.text: A request by the Russians to participate as co-plaintiffs in the Hamburg trial was rejected by the court. The company Gazprom, which owns the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, had argued its right to do so due to what it has referred to as the severe economic consequences resulting from the attack. The court argued that while repair costs of the pipelines would be high, it would not be economically impossible to restore them.

According to reports, Kuznetsov, whose military ID indicates he was in active military service at the time the pipelines were blown up, is expected to maintain his right to remain silent during the trial.
His legal team is expected to produce affidavits from two of his military superiors to support the argument that he is prohibited from revealing details of his actions as a soldier.
He is reported to have allegedly taken his orders from a man who is considered to be the mastermind behind the attack and is one of those who has sworn in his favour.
Sixteen trial dates have been scheduled at Hamburg’s Hanseatic higher regional court up to and including 17 December, with further hearings likely in January and February.

articles.title: Trump to fly to Manila for ASEAN summit, first PH visit since 2017
articles.summary: It will be Trump’s first visit since 2017, when the Philippines last hosted the ASEAN summit.

blocks.text: October 14, 2026 | 1:58pm
A composite photo of US President Donald Trump and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
AFP / PPA
MANILA, Philippines — United States President Donald Trump will attend the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila next month, Malacañang confirmed on Wednesday, October 14.
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said during a briefing today the US leader's visit was now "confirmed."
It will be Trump’s first visit since 2017, when the Philippines last hosted the ASEAN summit.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. extended the invitation to Trump during his White House visit in July 2025. “I look forward to hosting President Trump next year to attend the ASEAN meetings,” Marcos said in his arrival statement after the trip.

The Philippines chairs ASEAN this year and will host the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from November 16 to 18, with the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City as the main venue.
The three days have been declared special non-working days in Metro Manila due to the anticipated traffic and for the security of the summit participants.
Trump will join the summit and then fly to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit from November 17 to 19, according to reports citing the White House.

articles.title: Australian industry reliant on gas for ‘foreseeable future’, resources minister tells press club
articles.summary:
Madeleine King says national gas reservation scheme, expected to come into effect from 2028, will reduce power prices

  • Follow our

blocks.text: The resources minister, Madeleine King, says Australian industry will be reliant on gas for the “foreseeable future”, and that the national gas reservation scheme will push down power prices.

But the Western Australian MP did not put a price tag on the cost of gas under the proposal– as the former opposition leader, Peter Dutton, once did – nor predict when households and businesses would start to see that financial relief.
The national gas reservation scheme will force gas companies to set aside 20% of exports for domestic use, and is expected to come into effect from January 2028.

It will give the Australian Energy Regulator the power to force companies to meet a target of 110% of projected demand each year. It will also limit ministerial discretion and replace the Turnbull-era domestic gas security mechanism.
In an address to the National Press Club on Wednesday, King said keeping gas affordable for households and businesses was a critical part of the scheme’s primary focus.
“We expect the oversupply part of the reservation to put that modest oversupply into the system, which will push down those prices,” she said.
“So we do expect to see that downward pressure on prices. It’s a very important aspect of the whole scheme.”
The minister said gas was central to heating homes, keeping manufacturing industries running, processing critical minerals and rare earths domestically and supporting the rollout of renewables.
King said gas would continue to play an important role well into the future without a viable replacement.

“The truth is, it’s hard to establish a date because we don’t yet have the replacement for some of the industries that will that need it,” she said.

“Right now, there is no replacement for gas. I am totally supportive of any kind of research or development that finds a replacement, whether it’s just in lower emissions or alternative. But right now, and for the foreseeable future, that does not exist.”

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: ​Why small boat crossings are here to stay ​
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The ​collapse of the UK’s ‘one in, one out’ asylum deal with France exposes the limits of border enforcement that did little to stop crossings, and only made them more…

blocks.text: Good morning. You’d be forgiven for missing it. Earlier this month, the government quietly scrapped its “one in, one out” deal with France. The partnership was supposed to eliminate small boat crossings by deterring asylum seekers from making the treacherous journey across the world’s busiest shipping channel.

The deal, which lasted just 423 days, was beset with problems, had a negligible impact, and now joins a long list of policies that have tried and failed to address highly visible, often tragic small boat crossings. This morning, the Home Office announced that it would be doubling the number of riot police along the French coast in lieu of the deal.

Although small boat arrivals have actually decreased over the last year, the far right continues to weaponise these crossings. In its annual threat briefing yesterday, the head of MI5 warned that extremists with anti-immigration opinions are increasingly considering carrying out terrorist attacks.

Today’s newsletter speaks to specialist reporter Diane Taylor and Daniel Trilling, author of If We Tolerate This, to situate the deal’s collapse within the wider context of policies that have exacerbated the sense of disorder they’re supposed to resolve – and asks what comes next. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK news | Extremists holding anti-immigration opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels, the head of MI5 has warned.
UK politics | Nigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against small boat crossings in the Channel.

Ukraine | Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.
US politics | Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.

Pope Leo XIV | Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican said late on Tuesday. Leo, 71, underwent an operation and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, with tests confirming a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘I’ve never seen as much suffering caused to refugees by government policy’

blocks.caption: Policies that do not allow for safe routes put asylum seekers in more danger. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA

blocks.text: The one in, one out policy that was announced in a joint press conference between Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron in July last year was supposed to render small boat crossings pointless. A person arriving in a small boat to the UK could be forcibly returned to France in exchange for another person who would be brought legally to the UK. “In effect,” Diane Taylor wrote in a moving piece about the scheme in September, asylum seekers were “used as reluctant human shields to protect our borders from others in the same predicament.”

The scheme was always limited in scale; of the 40,000 people who arrived in small boats while it was active, just 1,500 – roughly 4% – were returned to France. A report by British Future, a thinktank that championed the policy, recognised that it would have to be expanded twenty-fold to close down routes as a viable way to claim asylum. But it’s doubtful that, even at this far larger scale, it would have ever been effective. Diane reported in August that nearly 50 asylum seekers deported under the scheme returned to the UK a second time, and an unknown number arrived undetected.

The government would have liked the scheme to continue, and its official explanation was that it was scrapped because it couldn’t be effectively scaled up. But it seems likely that political concerns in France also played a role. “At a time when immigration is going to be a major issue in the French presidential election, France doesn’t want to be seen to be taking in more unwanted people from the UK,” Rajeev Syal, the Guardian’s home affairs editor, tells me.
The other side of one in, one out

The deal was partially founded on a recognition of the need for safer routes to claim asylum in Britain. Starmer acknowledged when announcing it that “it is right that we offer a haven to those in most dire need”. But this flicker of humanitarianism was outweighed by the scheme’s arbitrary cruelty. Nearly 100 children were misidentified as adults and wrongly detained under the scheme, while some asylum seekers deported back to France were beaten by people smugglers. “I’ve been writing about asylum seekers for 25 years and I’ve never seen as much suffering caused to refugees by a UK government policy,” says Diane.

It was also accompanied by the government’s fortification of security measures along the French border. To some extent, these security measures help to explain the drop in small boat crossings this year, together with an overall reduction in arrivals of asylum seekers to Europe. But they have also encouraged people to make even more unsafe crossings. The increased police presence in northern France has led to more trips in larger “mega-dinghies”, which became a subject of panicked headlines this summer, as smugglers attempt to transport more people in single crossings.

Increased security has also encouraged people to take longer routes across the channel, sailing from Normandy and Belgium rather than Calais. Earlier this summer, far-right protests spread to Portsmouth, where people arriving on small boats had sailed from Normandy. “In effect, while the security measures seem on the surface to be working, they also contribute to boat journeys becoming far more dangerous, again adding to the sense of spectacle,” Daniel Trilling tells me.
Why are so many people still crossing in small boats?

The right frames small boat crossings as a failure to control immigration. Crucially, though, they’re a manifestation of ever-more draconian attempts to crack down on people trying to claim asylum in the UK. Before people crossed the channel in dinghies, they hid in lorries, or took flights to the UK using false passports. “When I first started reporting in Calais in 2014, it was still possible for refugees to stow themselves away on lorries without paying smugglers for access,” Daniel recalls. “But the more security that was placed around ports, the harder that became, and the more refugees had to rely on smugglers who could get access to secure lorry parks.”

In 2020, when the pandemic temporarily grounded traffic between Calais and Britain, small boat crossings spiked dramatically. By the following year, these crossings had more than doubled. “There used to be really, really small numbers of boats arriving in Britain, and nobody paid attention to them,” Diane says. “And obviously, you didn’t get far-right influencers live-streaming arrivals at border control in Heathrow, or standing on the hard shoulder of the M25 waiting to film asylum seekers for their YouTube.”
What happens next

Part of the calculation behind the government’s latest decision to double the number of riot police in northern France is that, now the deal has ended, it has limited time in which to strengthen its partnership with the French government. If Marine Le Pen is elected in April next year, it’s plausible that her government could refuse to take any asylum seekers from Britain, further politicising the issue and causing a rise in crossings that would play into the hands of the far right here.

Yet the decision is also yet another manifestation of the tendency to treat migration as a security issue rather than a reflection of an increasingly unstable world. No matter the increase in security or threats of deportation, people will keep trying to claim asylum. “As long as we have wars, instability and persecution, people will be displaced, and we need to work out ways to respond to that, rather than pretending that a policy tweak here or extra security measure there will simply make it disappear,” Daniel says. “At some point, you have to make a political argument for why asylum isn’t just an act of generosity, but a necessary response to the world as it is.”

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Peter receiving a certificate with his reading coach Alison Hollinrake. Photograph: Supplied image

blocks.text: Peter Lloyd spent most of his life unable to read or write, despite repeated attempts to learn. He struggled in school, left with no qualifications, and developed coping strategies that enabled him to work successfully as a lorry driver. During the Covid lockdowns, he found that it had become an overwhelming issue, particularly when he could not help home-school his son.
Encouraged by his wife, he contacted the charity Read Easy and began lessons with a volunteer tutor. Over three years, he learned to read and now Lloyd serves as a Read Easy ambassador.

Lloyd says: “I think it’s important to encourage others in my situation to seek help, especially men who might be too ashamed. I have three books on the go at the moment – I can’t believe how beautiful reading is!”

articles.title: Makabayan groups decry dropping of Sara confidential funds charge
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson assailed the Senate on Wednesday, October 14, for what he claims was more than P500 million in "wasted" public funds after three of four impeachment…

blocks.text: October 14, 2026 | 1:43pm

MANILA, Philippines — Progressive groups that have pushed for Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment criticized the House prosecution on Wednesday, October 14, for dropping the charge over her alleged misuse of confidential funds, an issue that the Makabayan bloc was the first to raise in a Romualdez-led Congress in 2023.

The Senate impeachment court yesterday allowed prosecutors to withdraw three of their four articles of impeachment, including Article I, which accused Duterte of misusing P612.5 million in confidential funds at the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education. Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero ruled the charge withdrawn with prejudice, meaning the House cannot revive it against Duterte during her current term.
The prosecution now stands only on Article II, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth.
'Absence of accountability'
Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) president Renato Reyes Jr. rejected the prosecution’s argument that narrowing the case would speed up the trial.
“Our impatience is not with the length of the trial but with the repeated absence of accountability of our top officials,” Reyes said in a statement on Wednesday.
Reyes said groups that backed the impeachment wanted closure on the confidential funds issue, and that a “judgement should have been rendered on this long-standing corruption issue.”

He also cited what he called President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s flip-flopping on the first impeachment, selective prosecution in the flood control scandal, and the fight over the Senate leadership, which he tied to the trial.

Reyes said progressive groups had filed impeachment complaints against Duterte in 2024 and 2026, and one against Marcos over alleged budget insertion kickbacks and flood control corruption. He said Duterte would “most likely” be convicted this year, but that her removal would not vindicate the justice system while other officials, “Marcos Jr included,” escape accountability.
Former ACT Teachers Party-list Rep. France Castro, who questioned the OVP’s confidential fund spending during budget deliberations in 2023, said the evidence on the charge was clear.

“Malinaw ang mga ebidensya — milyun-milyong confidential funds na ginastos sa loob lamang ng ilang araw, walang maayos na liquidation, at mga pinakitang mga resibo ay hindi kapani-paniwala. Hindi pwedeng basta na lamang burahin ang isyu ng pananagutan,” Castro said in a statement. (The evidence is clear: millions in confidential funds spent in just a few days, no proper liquidation, and receipts that are not believable. The issue of accountability cannot simply be erased.)

In August 2023, the House appropriations committee ended its hearing on the OVP’s proposed 2024 budget right after Duterte’s presentation without subjecting her office's spending to scrutiny. The motion to end it came from then-Senior Deputy Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, the president’s son, who cited “parliamentary courtesy" to the vice president.

Castro and fellow Makabayan lawmakers Rep. Raoul Manuel (Kabataan) and Rep. Arlene Brosas (Gabriela) were the only House members who criticized the move at the time and stressed the need to press Duterte over her office's confidential spending. But they were outnumbered by the 21 committee members who moved to terminate the hearing after less than an hour.

On Wednesday, Castro raised: “Are they worried that this issue would boomerang to President Marcos? Tandaan natin: si Marcos mismo ang nagbigay ng confidential funds kay VP Duterte noong 2022,” she said. (Let us remember: Marcos himself gave the confidential funds to VP Duterte in 2022.)
The OVP received P125 million in confidential funds in 2022 through a transfer from the Office of the President.
Prosecution: One article is enough

Lead prosecutor Rep. Jinky Luistro (Batangas, 2nd District) told the court yesterday that the unexplained-wealth evidence was enough on its own to remove Duterte. She said narrowing the case would shorten the trial and benefit the Senate, the respondent and the public.
She said the panel still considers all four charges equally strong.

The prosecution’s final witness, forensic financial analyst Alexander Cabrera, testified that Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, had P817.87 million in undeclared assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

Escudero said prosecutors who drop charges after resting their case “must therefore accept the legal consequences.” The bribery charge (Article III) was dropped without prejudice because no evidence had been presented on it.
The court also ruled that the defense need not present evidence on the three dropped articles, and Escudero lifted the gag on public discussion of them.
Duterte camp: A waste of public funds

Duterte’s camp also objected to the withdrawal, with the vice president's spokesperson, lawyer Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr., saying millions had been "wasted" after 20 trial days were spent on Articles I and IV, the grave threats charge.

“That is approximately P25 million in Senate operating cost per day, or P500 million of taxpayers’ money, consumed on charges that will never be voted on,” he said. Panelo claimed the total would exceed P1 billion once lawmakers’ salaries, lawyers, consultants, "content creators" and the House justice panel’s hearings were added. He did not say where his figures came from.

The P25 million is what the Senate spends each day on electricity, utilities and salaries, with or without a trial, according to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, who cited the figure in June. On July 16, he explained that the trial incurred the Senate no additional cost because it is handled like a plenary session.

Panelo argued the withdrawal was “an admission that the allegations lacked basis from the very beginning.” He said it denied Duterte the chance to rebut the evidence and win “the vindication of the acquittal she deserves.”
He also asked whether the Senate majority had kept quiet because the votes to convict Duterte were “already locked in under the lower threshold.”
“The silence is deafening,” Panelo said. “Huwag naman kayong masyadong halata.” (Don’t make it so obvious.)

The defense did not oppose the withdrawal itself but objected to losing the chance to answer the evidence already presented. “[The prosecution] presented their evidence. The court allowed them time, gave them opportunity, gave them platform, but now since they withdrew, your vice president can no longer speak or defend herself from those allegations,” lead defense counsel Sheila Sison said.
Escudero stood by his ruling and said: "No useful adjudicative purpose will be served by receiving evidence directed solely against charges that have already been withdrawn.”

Conviction would remove Duterte from office and permanently bar her from public office. She has denied wrongdoing and calls the case politically motivated, saying it is meant to damage her ahead of the 2028 elections.
The trial resumes on November 9, when the defense begins presenting its evidence.

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte won't resign? Malacañang says that's her decision
articles.summary: Malacañang said Wednesday nobody will interfere with the decision of Vice President Sara Duterte to remain on her post amid her impeachment trial, shrugging off her pronouncement that she has no…

blocks.text: Published October 14, 2026 1:42pm

Malacañang said Wednesday nobody will interfere with the decision of Vice President Sara Duterte to remain on her post amid her impeachment trial, shrugging off her pronouncement that she has no intention of stepping down.
In a press briefing, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the only thing that is "ridiculous" is Duterte's call for President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. to resign.

"Wala siyang karapatan na humingi ng resignation ng Pangulo. Ang Pangulo ay nagtatrabaho. Ang Pangulo ay laging ang iniisip ay kapakanan ng bansa, kapakanan ng taumbayan. Hindi nagkakaroon ng anumang secret deal sa mga dayuhan para ipagkalulo ang interes ng ating mga kababayan," Castro said.

(She has no right to demand the President's resignation. The President is working. The President always thinks of the welfare of the country and the people. He does not enter into any secret deals with foreigners to sell out the interests of our fellow citizens.)
"Kung hindi po siya magre-resign, desisyon niya po 'yan. Walang manghihimasok diyan. Pero ang pagsasabi niya na mag-resign ang Pangulo, 'yan ay malaking kalokohan," she added.
(If she chooses not to resign, that is her decision. No one will interfere with that. But for her to say that the President should resign, that is utter nonsense.)
Duterte on Tuesday said she "will not resign, will never resign from the Office of the Vice President" amid her impeachment trial and the allegations against her.
Last month, the Vice President urged Marcos to step down from office following her rescheduled arraignment over her grave threats case. — VDV, GMA News
